newsitem.title: UK: Doctors call for whole new approach to cancer.
newsitem.headline: Doctors call for whole new approach to cancer.

text.p: The idea of killing cancer off with strong chemicals and radiation therapy is old-fashioned and should be replaced with an entirely different approach, a group of British and Canadian doctors proposed on Friday.
They said there could be a subtler and gentler, but ultimately more effective, way to manage cancer without subjecting patients to toxic chemicals and x-rays aimed at wholesale destruction.

They argued in a commentary in the Lancet medical journal that cancer should no longer be viewed as a "monster" that must be destroyed, but should instead be studied as a process that could be tackled in several different ways,

"We are not alone in the belief that the killing method, whilst having offered substantial advances, is not likely to lead to cure," Harvey Schipper and Eva Turley of the University of Manitoba and Michael Baum of University College London wrote.
"Rather than trying to cure cancer by killing off every last cell, it would make more sense to control the disease."

Schipper said in a telephone interview: "Cancer is a regulatory disease -- it is a disease of abnormal regulation. The process is very sensitive and the malignant process can be reversed without killing cancer cells."

The doctors said their approach, based on a large body of research by other experts, would tie together various strands of medicine with ideas borrowed from engineering and even from mathematics' fashionable new chaos theory.

"Where apparent cure is achieved, there is good evidence that other mechanisms are responsible," they wrote. Natural cell mechanisms such as apoptosis, or cell suicide, could be better harnessed to fight cancer, they said.
Many researchers believe that cancer occurs in part when apoptosis fails and damaged cells do not self-destruct but become essentially immortal.

Chaos theory teaches that tiny changes can have profound effects and Schipper said this could easily be shown in the case of apoptosis. He gave as an example doxorubicin, a powerful drug used against breast cancer and leukaemia.
"We invented it to kill but it turns out that when given at a very much lower dose (than normal) it does something much more profound and much subtler. It turns off the immortality," he said.
The new approach would involve seeing how doxorubicin re-set a cell's apoptosis mechanism.

The doctors said researchers should collect and analyse cancer cells. "In time, a library of cell colonies, representing the known metabolic defects associated with growth, invasion and metastasis (spreading), would be available," they said.

Careful monitoring and regulation might result in a more effective and less traumatic treatment. "This subtler approach to cancer treatment may reveal that we already know enough to achieve a more satisfactory result," they concluded.
Schipper said past methods had certainly been valuable and he did not want to imply that current ways of treating cancer were wrong.
"This doesn't mean that tomorrow morning we going to stop surgery, stop chemotherapy and stop radiation," he said.
"You are going to have a mix of trying to take as much of the tumour out as you can but at same time you don't want to set the whole thing off by upsetting the biological balance."
